l: Teancum, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Teancum leads Moroni's army against the people of Morianton at the narrow pass. He kills Morianton, defeats his army, takes them prisoners, and returns to Moroni's camp.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Pahoran, the son of Nephihah, is appointed chief judge and governor at the end of the twenty and fourth year. He is charged to judge righteously, preserve peace and freedom, protect sacred worship, support the cause of God, and bring the wicked to justice.

l: Lord, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The Lord delivers those who faithfully keep his commandments, while wicked people are consigned to bondage, perish by the sword, or dwindle in unbelief.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The Nephites build cities and defenses, expand their possessions, and prosper greatly. They experience peace until the contention over the lands of Lehi and Morianton, and peace is restored after Morianton's defeat.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The Lamanites are driven from the east wilderness and lose strongholds in the east and west. Their lands are separated from the Nephites by fortified lines.

l: people of Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The people of Morianton claim part of the land of Lehi, take up arms, and flee northward after seeking to avoid Moroni's army. They are defeated, taken prisoners, and restored to their land after covenanting to keep the peace.

l: people of Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The people of Lehi flee to Moroni's camp and ask for assistance because they are not in the wrong. They are later restored to their lands and united with the people of Morianton.

l: Nephite armies, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The armies of the Nephites dig defensive earthworks, build timber protections and towers, drive the Lamanites from the east wilderness, occupy southern borders, and defeat Morianton's army.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The inhabitants of the land of Zarahemla go into the east wilderness to possess land by the seashore.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The land of Nephi runs in a straight course from the east sea to the west and lies south of the lands possessed by the Nephites.

l: east wilderness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The east wilderness is cleared of Lamanites and settled by inhabitants from the land of Zarahemla and surrounding areas. Moroni places armies and fortifications there.

l: land Bountiful, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The land Bountiful is where Moroni and his people are located when Moroni fears that Morianton will gain possession of land and threaten Nephite liberty.

l: city of Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The Nephites begin the foundation of the city of Moroni by the east sea and south of the Lamanite possessions.

l: land of Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The land of Lehi lies by the seashore and borders the land of Morianton. Its people flee to Moroni for protection during the conflict.

l: land of Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The land of Morianton borders the land of Lehi by the seashore. Its people are restored to it after they covenant to keep the peace.

l: land northward, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The land northward is covered with large bodies of water and is the destination Morianton plans to reach. Teancum stops the fleeing people at the pass leading into it.

l: fortifications, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Strongholds are prepared around every Nephite city to protect against the Lamanites and prevent them from retaining power in their lands.

l: fortifications, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Fortifications are erected in the east wilderness and along the line between the Nephites and Lamanites to secure the armies and people.

l: judgment-seat, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The judgment-seat is filled by Nephihah until his death and then by his son Pahoran, who begins his reign at the end of the twenty and fourth year.

l: war preparations, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Moroni continues making preparations for war by ordering defensive earthworks, timber structures, pickets, towers, and places of security around the cities.

l: defense against the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Defense against the Lamanites includes strongholds, armies, cleared wilderness, fortified borders, and protections that allow the Nephites to secure their cities and lands.

l: peace, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Peace characterizes the twenty and second and twenty and third years and is restored after the conflict involving Morianton. The people of Morianton covenant to keep the peace before returning to their land.

l: prosperity, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The Nephites prosper exceedingly, become rich, multiply, and grow strong because of their security and faithfulness.

l: commandments of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Keeping the commandments of the Lord brings prosperity and continued presence with him, while refusing them results in being cut off from his presence.

l: promises to Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The promises to Lehi are shown to be fulfilled: his children prosper when they keep the Lord's commandments and are cut off when they do not.

l: liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Nephite liberty is threatened by Morianton's planned migration and possible control of northern lands. Moroni acts to prevent consequences that could overthrow it.

l: battle between Teancum and Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: The battle begins when Morianton's stubborn people resist Moroni's army at the narrow pass. Teancum kills Morianton, defeats the army, and takes the people prisoners.

l: appointment of Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 50
s: Pahoran is appointed chief judge and governor after the death of his father, Nephihah. His appointment includes an oath and sacred ordinance to judge righteously and preserve peace and freedom.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The people of Nephi divide over whether the law should be altered and whether Pahoran should remain chief judge, but the freemen prevail by the voice of the people. Amalickiah leads the Lamanites in an invasion, captures several Nephite cities, and is stopped and killed by Teancum near the land Bountiful. Moroni suppresses the king-men, killing or imprisoning their leaders and compelling the remainder to defend their country. Teancum and his men then resist the Lamanites and place the title of liberty on their cities and towers.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Pahoran refuses to alter the law and remains chief judge after the voice of the people favors the freemen.

l: Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Amalickiah gathers and leads a Lamanite army against the Nephites, captures many cities, and is killed by Teancum with a javelin.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Moroni becomes exceedingly angry at the king-men's refusal to defend their country and leads action against them. He also prepares for war against the Lamanites.

l: Teancum, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Teancum repulses Amalickiah and the Lamanites at the borders of the land Bountiful. He later enters Amalickiah's tent at night and causes his death.

l: people of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The people of Nephi divide over the law and Pahoran, settle the matter by their voice, and face invasion by the Lamanites.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The Lamanites invade the Nephite lands under Amalickiah, capture many cities, and are driven back by Teancum and his men at the land Bountiful.

l: king-men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The king-men seek to dethrone Pahoran, alter the law, and establish a king. Moroni's army kills four thousand dissenters, imprisons leaders, and compels the remainder to support liberty.

l: freemen, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The freemen support Pahoran and a free government, prevail by the voice of the people, and put the king-men to silence.

l: Moroni's army, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Moroni's army attacks the king-men, killing or imprisoning their leaders and forcing the remainder to take up arms for their country.

l: Teancum's army, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Teancum's men repulse and harass the Lamanites, killing them until dark and camping near the borders of the land Bountiful.

l: Lamanite army, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The Lamanite army is gathered and led by Amalickiah, captures fortified Nephite cities, and is stopped by Teancum's men.

l: land of Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The land of Moroni is invaded by the Lamanites, who drive out the Nephites and take possession of its city and fortifications.

l: city of Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The city of Moroni is insufficiently defended, so Amalickiah captures it and its fortifications after many Nephites are slain.

l: city of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The people who flee the city of Moroni gather at the city of Nephihah and prepare to receive the Lamanites in battle.

l: land Bountiful, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The Lamanites march toward the land Bountiful but are met and repulsed by Teancum and his men at its borders.

l: law, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Some people seek to alter particular points of the law, but Pahoran refuses to allow the law to be altered.

l: liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The freemen covenant to maintain their rights and religious privileges through a free government, and the king-men's attempt to overthrow it is suppressed.

l: judgment-seat, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Pahoran retains the judgment-seat after the people favor the freemen, while the king-men's effort to remove him fails.

l: contention over the law, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The contention over the law concerns changing particular points and removing Pahoran as chief judge. It is settled without bloodshed by the voice of the people.

l: settlement by the voice of the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The people settle the dispute concerning Pahoran by their voice, favoring the freemen and allowing Pahoran to retain the judgment-seat.

l: Lamanite invasion, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The Lamanite invasion begins while the Nephites are divided over their government, and Amalickiah captures multiple cities before Teancum stops him.

l: war against the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Amalickiah prepares and leads the Lamanites in war against the Nephites after swearing to drink Moroni's blood.

l: execution of the king-men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Moroni's army executes four thousand king-men by the sword, while leaders not slain are imprisoned and the remainder submit to the standard of liberty.

l: capture of Nephite cities, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Amalickiah captures the cities of Moroni, Nephihah, Lehi, Morianton, Omner, Gid, and Mulek, gaining fortified strongholds along the seashore.

l: death of Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: Amalickiah dies when Teancum secretly enters his tent at night and puts a javelin to his heart.

l: title of liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 51
s: The remaining king-men are compelled to hoist the title of liberty upon their towers and in their cities and to take up arms in defense of their country.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Amalickiah is found dead in his tent, and his brother Ammoron becomes king over the Lamanites. Teancum and Moroni defend the Nephite lands, recover the city of Mulek through a stratagem, and defeat the Lamanite army led by Jacob. Jacob is killed, Moroni is wounded, and many Lamanites surrender their weapons and become prisoners. The Nephites take more prisoners than the number slain in the battle.

l: Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Amalickiah is found dead in his own tent on the first morning of the twenty and sixth year.

l: Teancum, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Teancum prepares to battle the Lamanites, defends his position, and receives orders from Moroni. He leads the Lamanites away from the city of Mulek, helping Moroni capture it.

l: Ammoron, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Ammoron, the brother of Amalickiah, is appointed king over the Lamanites. He commands his people to maintain the cities they have taken and leads forces against the Nephites.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Moroni strengthens Teancum’s army, orders the retention of prisoners, and directs the fortification of land Bountiful and its narrow pass. He captures the city of Mulek through a stratagem, fights Jacob’s forces, is wounded, and accepts the surrender of many Lamanites.

l: Jacob, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Jacob, a Zoramite, leads the Lamanite army protecting the city of Mulek. He refuses to meet the Nephites on the plains, leads his army against Teancum, and is killed in battle with Moroni.

l: Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Lehi and a small army protect the city Bountiful and meet the retreating Lamanites. He presses upon their rear, causing many to surrender their weapons.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: The Lamanites retreat into the city of Mulek and maintain the cities and lands they have taken. They pursue Teancum, are surrounded and defeated by Moroni and Lehi, and many surrender or are taken prisoner.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: The Nephites are defending their lands against Lamanite attacks on the west and east borders. Their armies recover the city of Mulek and defeat the Lamanites.

l: city of Mulek, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: The city of Mulek is held by the Lamanites under Jacob. Moroni captures it after Teancum decoys the Lamanite army away.

l: land Bountiful, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Moroni orders Teancum to fortify land Bountiful and secure the narrow pass leading into the land northward. The city Bountiful is protected by Lehi and a small army.

l: fortifications, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: The Lamanites seek protection in their fortifications, and Teancum decides not to attack them directly because of their strength. Moroni’s plan draws the Lamanites out of their strongholds.

l: cities, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: The Lamanites have taken and seek to maintain several cities after suffering much bloodshed. Moroni directs the Nephites to retake the city of Mulek and strengthen the surrounding cities.

l: prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Moroni orders Teancum to retain Lamanite prisoners as a ransom for Nephite prisoners taken by the Lamanites. After the battle, the number of prisoners exceeds the number slain on both sides.

l: swords, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Moroni commands the Lamanites to surrender their weapons of war. Many throw down their weapons, while others are taken and bound and compelled to march into the land Bountiful.

l: armies, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Moroni, Teancum, and Lehi command Nephite armies in coordinated actions against the Lamanites. The Lamanite armies pursue Teancum, are surrounded, and are overpowered by fresh Nephite forces.

l: war against the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: The battle involves Moroni’s and Lehi’s forces against the Lamanites led by Jacob. Many are slain, Moroni is wounded, Jacob is killed, and the surviving Lamanites surrender or are captured.

l: death of Amalickiah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: The death of Amalickiah is discovered by the Lamanites in his own tent. His death leads to Ammoron being appointed king.

l: war preparations, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Teancum prepares walls and places of resort to defend his men. Moroni orders the defense and strengthening of land Bountiful, its narrow pass, and nearby cities.

l: stratagem, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 52
s: Moroni uses a stratagem in which Teancum leads a small force along the seashore while Moroni’s army approaches the city of Mulek from the wilderness. The plan causes the Lamanites to leave the city, allowing Moroni to capture it.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Moroni places Lamanite prisoners under guard, has them bury the dead, and makes them build fortifications around the land Bountiful after capturing the city of Mulek with Lehi. Moroni prepares the Nephites for war and protects their women and children, while armies of the Lamanites gain several cities on the west sea because of dissensions and intrigue among the Nephites. The people of Ammon want to take up arms to defend the Nephites but are restrained by Helaman because of their oath against shedding blood. Two thousand of their sons form a covenant to defend the Nephites and choose Helaman as their leader.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Moroni places men to guard Lamanite prisoners while they bury the dead and labor. He takes command of the city of Mulek with Lehi, gives the city to Lehi, and has the prisoners build fortifications around the land Bountiful. He prepares his men for war, protects women and children from famine and affliction, and does not attempt another battle that year.

l: Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Lehi goes with Moroni to the city of Mulek and receives command of it. He has been with Moroni in most of his battles, and he and Moroni rejoice in each other’s safety.

l: Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Helaman and his brethren persuade the people of Ammon not to take up weapons and break their oath. He leads the two thousand young men who covenant to defend the Nephites and marches with them toward the southern borders by the west sea.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The Lamanites bury their dead and the dead Nephites, then labor under Moroni’s orders to build a ditch, breastwork, and wall around the land Bountiful. Their prisoners are guarded within the fortification they build.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The Nephites protect the people of Ammon and suffer afflictions and tribulations while defending them. Dissensions and intrigue among them put them in dangerous circumstances, and armies of the Lamanites gain possession of several Nephite cities in the west.

l: people of Anti-Nephi-Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The people of Ammon, formerly Lamanites, were converted unto the Lord by Ammon and his brethren and have been protected by the Nephites. Moved by compassion for the Nephites, they desire to take up arms, but Helaman persuades them not to break their oath.

l: sons of the people of Ammon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Two thousand young men of the people of Ammon, who are not bound by the oath against shedding blood, enter a covenant to fight for the liberty of the Nephites and protect the land. They are valiant, strong, active, truthful, sober, and taught to keep the commandments of God, and they choose Helaman as their leader.

l: armies of the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The armies of the Lamanites on the west sea gain ground over the Nephites while Moroni is absent because of intrigue among the Nephites. They obtain possession of a number of Nephite cities in that part of the land.

l: city of Mulek, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The city of Mulek is taken by Moroni and given to Lehi. It is described as one of the strongest holds of the Lamanites in the land of Nephi.

l: land Bountiful, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The Lamanite prisoners are marched back into the land Bountiful and forced to dig a ditch and build a strong wall around the city. The land becomes an exceeding stronghold, and the prisoners are guarded there.

l: oath against shedding blood, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The people of Ammon have taken an oath that they will never shed blood again. Because of this oath, they are restrained from taking up weapons even when they want to defend the Nephites.

l: covenant to defend the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Two thousand young men enter a covenant to fight for the liberty of the Nephites, protect the land, and defend the Nephites and themselves from bondage. They covenant never to give up their liberty.

l: victory over the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Moroni gains a victory over one of the greatest armies of the Lamanites and obtains possession of the city of Mulek.

l: war preparations, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Moroni employs his men in preparing for war and making fortifications against the Lamanites. He also provides food for the armies and delivers women and children from famine and affliction.

l: dissensions and intrigue, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: Dissensions and intrigue among the Nephites cause Moroni to be absent and place the Nephites in dangerous circumstances. They enable the armies of the Lamanites on the west sea to gain ground and capture several cities.

l: bondage, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The young men covenant to protect the Nephites and themselves from bondage.

l: liberty of the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 53
s: The two thousand young men covenant to fight for the liberty of the Nephites and never give it up.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: At the commencement of the twenty and ninth year of the judges, Ammoron asked Moroni to exchange prisoners. Moroni agreed only if Ammoron would deliver a man, his wife, and his children for one prisoner, while threatening to fight if Ammoron refused. Moroni and Ammoron exchanged epistles concerning the war, the justice of God, their peoples, and control of the government. Ammoron agreed to exchange prisoners but declared that the war would continue until the Nephites were subjected or eternally extinguished.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Moroni rejoiced at Ammoron's request to exchange prisoners because he desired the provisions used to support the Lamanite prisoners and wanted his own people to strengthen his army. He sent an epistle to Ammoron, warned him of God's wrath, and offered to exchange prisoners only if a man, his wife, and his children were given for one prisoner.

l: Ammoron, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Ammoron sent Moroni a request to exchange prisoners and later wrote an epistle in response to Moroni. He agreed to exchange prisoners to preserve food for his men of war, but declared that the war would continue until the Nephites were subjected to Lamanite authority or eternally extinguished.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: The Lamanites had taken many women and children, and they held prisoners whom Moroni sought to obtain through an exchange. Ammoron identified himself as their king and said that they would continue the war against the Nephites.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: The Nephites were the people whom Ammoron sought to subject to Lamanite authority or eternally extinguish. Moroni said that the Nephites would retain their cities and lands, maintain their religion and the cause of their God, and defend themselves.

l: prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: The prisoners were involved in the proposed exchange between Moroni and Ammoron. Moroni had prisoners but no women or children among them, and he required a Lamanite man, his wife, and his children for each prisoner he would exchange.

l: armies, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Moroni threatened to bring his armies against Ammoron if Ammoron did not withdraw, and said he would follow him into his own land. Ammoron also threatened to come against Moroni with his armies.

l: people of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Moroni said that Ammoron and his brother had waged war against the people of the Nephites. He said that his people had sought only to defend themselves and would seek to destroy the Lamanites if they continued trying to destroy them.

l: war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: The war had been waged against the Nephites and was still being continued after Amalickiah's death. Moroni said it concerned the defense of the Nephites, while Ammoron said it was to avenge wrongs and obtain and maintain rights to the government.

l: prisoner exchange, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Ammoron asked Moroni to exchange prisoners. Moroni set the condition that one man, his wife, and his children be delivered for one prisoner, and Ammoron agreed to exchange prisoners according to that request.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Moroni warned Ammoron about the justice of God and the sword of his almighty wrath if Ammoron did not repent and withdraw his armies. Ammoron said that he did not know such a being, and that if such a being existed, he might have made the Lamanites as well as the Nephites.

l: land of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: The land of Nephi was identified by Moroni as the land of Ammoron's possessions and the land to which Ammoron should return with his armies.

l: land of our first inheritance, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Moroni called the land of the Nephites their land of first inheritance and said that he would follow Ammoron into his own land. He also said that the Nephites would seek this land if the Lamanites continued trying to destroy them.

l: Moroni's epistle, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Moroni wrote an epistle to Ammoron concerning the war, God's justice, repentance, withdrawal, and the exchange of prisoners. Ammoron answered with another epistle about his identity, the alleged wrongs of the fathers, the government, the war, and the exchange of prisoners.

l: government, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 54
s: Ammoron claimed that the government rightly belonged to those whom the Nephites' fathers had robbed of it. He offered peace if the Nephites laid down their arms and submitted to those he said had the rightful government.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Moroni refuses to exchange prisoners with Ammoron and sends Laman to deceive the Lamanite guards at city Gid with wine. After the Lamanites become drunk and fall asleep, Moroni arms the Nephite prisoners, surrounds the city, captures the Lamanites, and takes possession of city Gid. He liberates the Nephite prisoners, strengthens the city’s fortifications, and sends the Lamanite prisoners to city Bountiful. The Nephites regain ground and begin winning victories, while Moroni prepares to attack city Morianton.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Moroni refuses to exchange prisoners unless Ammoron withdraws his purpose, and he plans to seek death among the Lamanites until they sue for peace. He uses Laman’s deception to arm the Nephite prisoners and capture city Gid, but he does not kill the drunken Lamanites because he does not delight in murder or bloodshed.

l: Ammoron, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Ammoron has a perfect knowledge of the fraud concerning the war against the people of Nephi. He refuses to grant Moroni’s epistle, so Moroni refuses to exchange prisoners with him.

l: Laman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Laman, a descendant of Laman and former servant of the king murdered by Amalickiah, goes with a small number of men to the guards over the Nephites. He claims that he and his men escaped from the Nephites with wine, leading the Lamanites to drink until they become drunk.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: The Nephites arm their prisoners inside city Gid, surround the Lamanites, and regain control of the city. They protect their prisoners, resist attempts involving wine, and begin again to be victorious and reclaim their rights and privileges.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: The Lamanites guarding the Nephites at city Gid drink the wine offered by Laman and become drunk and fall into a deep sleep. They surrender their weapons when surrounded, later attempt encirclements and the use of wine against the Nephites, and continue fortifying city Morianton.

l: armies of the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Moroni’s army is prepared with weapons of war and surrounds the Lamanite forces outside city Gid. It gains strength when the liberated Nephite prisoners join it.

l: Nephite prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: The Nephite prisoners in city Gid receive weapons of war from Moroni and gain possession of the parts within the walls. They are then liberated and join Moroni’s army.

l: prisoners of the Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: The Lamanite prisoners captured at city Gid are made to labor in strengthening the fortifications around the city. After city Gid is fortified, they are taken to city Bountiful and guarded there.

l: city of Gid, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: City Gid is the place where the Nephites are guarded by the Lamanites. Moroni captures it after arming the prisoners and surrounding the Lamanites, then strengthens its fortifications.

l: city of Morianton, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: The Lamanites fortify city Morianton until it becomes an exceedingly stronghold, continually bringing new forces and provisions there. Moroni prepares to attack it.

l: war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Ammoron wages the war against the people of Nephi without a just cause, according to Moroni. The conflict continues as Moroni seeks to force the Lamanites to sue for peace.

l: wine, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Laman uses wine to make the Lamanite guards believe that he and his men escaped from the Nephites. The Lamanites drink it freely until they are drunk, and later the Nephites test wine on Lamanite prisoners to guard against poison.

l: weapons of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Moroni’s men cast weapons of war to the Nephite prisoners in city Gid, arming them in silence. The Lamanites surrender their weapons by casting them at the feet of the Nephites.

l: fortifications, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Moroni causes the Lamanite prisoners to strengthen the fortifications around city Gid. The Lamanites also fortify city Morianton until it becomes an exceedingly stronghold.

l: poison, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: The Nephites are cautious that poison is not administered through wine. They give wine first to some Lamanite prisoners because wine poisonous to a Lamanite would also poison a Nephite.

l: saving the Nephites from destruction, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Moroni does not attack and destroy the drunken Lamanites because he delights in saving his people from destruction and does not want to bring injustice upon himself.

l: capture of city Gid, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: Moroni captures city Gid by arming the Nephite prisoners, surrounding the Lamanite army, and causing the Lamanites to surrender their weapons.

l: liberation of Nephite prisoners, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: After taking possession of city Gid, Moroni causes all the Nephite prisoners there to be liberated. They join Moroni’s army and become a great strength to it.

l: Nephite victories, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 55
s: The Nephites begin again to be victorious and reclaim their rights and privileges. They withstand nighttime encirclement attempts and efforts to use wine against them.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Helaman writes to Moroni about the warfare in his part of the land and the defense of Judea. Two thousand young descendants of Laman, called Helaman’s sons and stripling Ammonites, join the army of Antipus, which faces the Lamanites. Helaman leads a stratagem that draws the strongest Lamanite army away from Antiparah, allowing the army of Antipus and Helaman’s force to surround and capture them. None of the two thousand young men falls, and the prisoners of war are sent toward Zarahemla while Helaman returns with the remaining forces to Judea.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Moroni receives an epistle from Helaman concerning the affairs of the people and the warfare in Helaman’s part of the land.

l: Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Helaman leads two thousand young men in defense of their country, joins them to the army of Antipus, and directs a stratagem against the Lamanites. He returns with the young men to the battle, helps surround and defeat the Lamanites, finds that none of the two thousand has fallen, and returns toward Judea.

l: Antipus, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Antipus leads the army defending Judea and works to fortify the city. He orders Helaman to march near Antiparah and pursues the Lamanites, but he falls by the sword during the battle.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: God is understood by Helaman and the young men to have strengthened and preserved them. The young men believe that God will not suffer them to fall, and Helaman says they fought with the strength and power of God.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The Nephites defend their country and cities against the Lamanites. The people of Nephi join the people of Antipus and Helaman’s two thousand to surround and defeat the Lamanites.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The Lamanites possess Manti, Zeezrom, Cumeni, and Antiparah after shedding the blood of many Nephite men. Their strongest army pursues Helaman’s force, is surrounded, and surrenders its weapons of war and its members as prisoners of war.

l: sons of the people of Ammon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The stripling Ammonites are two thousand young descendants of Laman who take up weapons of war to defend their country. They follow Helaman into battle despite having never fought before, and none of them is killed.

l: army of Antipus, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The army of Antipus defends Judea, pursues the Lamanites, and joins Helaman’s force in surrounding and defeating them. It suffers the loss of Antipus and many leaders during the battle.

l: mothers, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The mothers of the two thousand young men teach them that God will deliver them if they do not doubt. The young men repeat their mothers’ words to Helaman before going into battle.

l: Judea, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Judea is the city where Helaman joins Antipus and his army. Its defenders fortify it, use it as a base for watching the Lamanites, and return to it after the battle.

l: city of Antiparah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Antiparah contains the strongest and most numerous Lamanite army in the area. Helaman’s force marches near it and draws that army away in pursuit.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Zarahemla sends two thousand men to support Helaman’s forces. The captured prisoners of war and some surviving men of Antipus are sent to the land of Zarahemla.

l: warfare, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The warfare concerns the defense of Nephite cities against Lamanite forces. It includes fortifying cities, watching enemy movements, conducting a stratagem, pursuing armies, and capturing prisoners.

l: covenant, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The fathers of the two thousand young men made a covenant not to take up weapons of war against their brethren to shed blood. Helaman previously would not allow the young men to break that covenant, although they later take up weapons to defend their country.

l: weapons of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The two thousand young men take up weapons of war to defend their country. The captured Lamanites surrender their weapons of war along with themselves as prisoners of war.

l: provisions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: Provisions are sent from the fathers of the two thousand young men, and additional provisions arrive to support the forces, their wives, and their children. Helaman’s march near Antiparah is presented as if he were carrying provisions to another city.

l: prisoners of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: The Lamanite army surrenders as prisoners of war after being surrounded by the people of Nephi, the people of Antipus, and Helaman’s two thousand. The prisoners are sent to the land of Zarahemla because Helaman’s forces have no place to guard them.

l: battle, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 56
s: A terrible battle begins after the army of Antipus overtakes the Lamanites. Antipus and many leaders fall, but Helaman’s return enables the Nephite forces to surround the Lamanites and compel their surrender.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Helaman rejects Ammoron's offer to exchange prisoners of war for the city of Antiparah, and Antiparah falls into Nephite hands after its people flee. In the twenty-ninth year, Helaman's army surrounds Cumeni, captures its provisions, and eventually obtains the city after the Lamanites lose hope of support. A Lamanite attack causes prisoners to rebel, but Helaman's two thousand and sixty sons of the Ammonites and the men escorting the prisoners help preserve Cumeni. Two hundred of the two thousand and sixty are wounded but all survive, which Helaman attributes to their faith and the miraculous power of God.

l: Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Helaman receives and rejects Ammoron's proposal to exchange prisoners for Antiparah, commands the Nephite forces around Cumeni, and records their victories and losses. He attributes the preservation of the two thousand and sixty to their faith and the miraculous power of God.

l: Ammoron, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Ammoron offers to deliver Antiparah if Helaman will surrender the prisoners of war, but refuses Helaman's proposed exchange. He later sends provisions and a numerous army to support the Lamanites at Cumeni.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: God is credited with delivering Helaman's forces from their enemies and preserving them from complete destruction. Helaman ascribes the survival of the two thousand and sixty to God's miraculous power.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: The Nephites capture Antiparah, surround and obtain Cumeni, and suffer substantial losses in battle. They retain Cumeni after defeating the Lamanites.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: The Lamanites abandon Antiparah, defend Cumeni, attempt repeated night attacks, and later receive reinforcements. They lose Cumeni and are driven back to Manti after suffering defeat.

l: sons of the people of Ammon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Sixty sons of the Ammonites join their two thousand brethren in Helaman's army. The two thousand and sixty fight firmly, obey commands exactly, and help secure victory at Cumeni.

l: prisoners of war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: The prisoners of war are held by Helaman's forces and are intended to be sent to Zarahemla. Many rebel after hearing that the Lamanite armies are approaching; many are slain, while some escape.

l: city of Antiparah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Antiparah is offered to Helaman in exchange for prisoners, but the exchange is refused. Its people flee to other cities, allowing the city to fall into Nephite hands.

l: city Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Cumeni is surrounded by Helaman's forces, cut off from provisions, and eventually yielded by the Lamanites. The Nephites retain the city after repelling a later attack.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: The land of Zarahemla supplies provisions and six thousand men to Helaman's army. It is also the intended destination for the prisoners of war.

l: battle with the army protecting Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Helaman's forces desire to battle the army protecting Cumeni and surround the city by night before its defenders receive provisions.

l: capture of Antiparah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: The capture of Antiparah occurs after its people leave the city and flee to other fortified cities. The city consequently falls into Nephite hands.

l: siege of Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: During the siege of Cumeni, Helaman's forces camp around the city for many nights, guard against attacks, and capture an incoming supply of provisions. The Lamanites eventually surrender the city after losing hope of relief.

l: battle at Cumeni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: At the battle at Cumeni, the two thousand and sixty and the men returning with the prisoners check the Lamanites and drive them back to Manti. The Nephites retain Cumeni but suffer great loss, including a thousand slain.

l: preservation of the two thousand and sixty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: Two hundred of the two thousand and sixty faint from blood loss, but all survive despite receiving many wounds. Their preservation astonishes Helaman's army while a thousand other Nephites are slain.

l: faith in Christ, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: The two thousand and sixty have exceeding faith in what they were taught about a just God. Their faith is associated with their preservation and their exact obedience to every command.

l: miraculous power of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 57
s: The miraculous power of God is identified as the reason the wounded two thousand and sixty are preserved. Helaman connects this power with their exceeding faith and the goodness of God.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: Helaman and the Nephites sought to obtain the city of Manti while facing a more numerous Lamanite army and receiving little support from Zarahemla. After praying, they received assurances from the Lord God, used a stratagem involving Gid and Teomner, and captured Manti without shedding blood. The Lamanites fled, and the Nephites regained their cities and lands, though many women and children were taken prisoner. Helaman reported that the sons of the people of Ammon remained faithful and that he trusted God despite the weakness of the Nephite armies.

l: Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: Helaman led the Nephite effort to capture the city of Manti and sent an embassy to the governor requesting provisions and strength. He directed the stratagem using Gid and Teomner, reported the Nephites' victories and difficulties to Moroni, and closed his epistle.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The Nephites waited for provisions and reinforcements, prayed for strength, and advanced against the Lamanites near Manti. They used a stratagem to capture the city without bloodshed, regained their cities and lands, and remained small in number for defending their possessions.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The Lamanites were more numerous, received strength and provisions, and repeatedly attempted to destroy the Nephites. Their army pursued the retreating Nephites into the wilderness, lost Manti when Gid and Teomner attacked its guards, and later fled toward the land of Nephi after finding the Nephites prepared.

l: city of Manti, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The city of Manti was held by the Lamanites and guarded by only a few men when their main army pursued the Nephites. Gid and Teomner destroyed the guards and took possession of the city, and the Nephites later arrived before the Lamanite army and retained it.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The Lord God visited the Nephites with assurances that he would deliver them, spoke peace to their souls, and granted them great faith and hope. Helaman trusted him to preserve the Nephites' cities, lands, possessions, and liberty despite their weak armies.

l: sons of the people of Ammon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The sons of the people of Ammon were with Helaman in the city of Manti. Although they received many wounds, not one of them was slain, and they remained steadfast in liberty, remembered the Lord God, kept his statutes, judgments, and commandments, and had strong faith in prophecy.

l: cities, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The Nephites regained all the cities that had been taken by the Lamanites. Their armies were small for maintaining so many cities, and the people and families who had not been taken prisoner were returning to their homes.

l: lands, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The Nephites regained possession of their own lands and trusted in God for victory over them. At the end of the unit, they possessed their lands while the Lamanites had fled to the land of Nephi.

l: liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The sons of the people of Ammon stood fast in the liberty with which God had made them free. They continually remembered the Lord God and obeyed his statutes, judgments, and commandments.

l: deliverance, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The Nephites prayed for deliverance from their enemies and for strength to retain their cities, lands, possessions, wives, children, and liberty. The Lord God assured them of deliverance, and Helaman continued to trust that God would deliver them despite their weak armies.

l: stratagem to capture Manti, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: Helaman caused Gid and a small number of men to hide on one side of the wilderness and Teomner and others to hide on the other side. After Helaman's army drew the Lamanites away, Gid and Teomner cut off the spies, attacked the city's guards, and captured Manti; Helaman's army then returned by night and took the city without bloodshed.

l: victory, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 58
s: The Nephites obtained victory over the lands that had been taken from them and regained their cities and possessions. Helaman attributed their success to God and trusted that further deliverance would come notwithstanding the weakness of their armies.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Moroni rejoices at Helaman’s success in regaining lost lands and tells his people to rejoice. He sends an epistle to Pahoran requesting men to strengthen Helaman’s armies, then plans to recover the remaining cities taken by the Lamanites. The Lamanites attack the people of Nephihah, slaughter many, and force the survivors to join Moroni’s army. After Nephihah is lost, Moroni and his chief captains sorrow, doubt because of the wickedness of the people, and Moroni becomes angry with the government for its indifference to the freedom of their country.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Moroni rejoices at Helaman’s success, informs his people so they may rejoice, and sends an epistle to Pahoran requesting men to strengthen Helaman’s armies. He plans to recover the remaining possessions and cities taken by the Lamanites, but retains his force elsewhere and fails to prevent the loss of Nephihah. He becomes exceedingly sorrowful, doubts because of the wickedness of the people, and is angry with the government.

l: Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Helaman has had exceeding success in obtaining the lands that were lost. Moroni requests that men be gathered to strengthen Helaman’s armies so they can maintain those lands.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Pahoran receives an epistle from Moroni requesting that he cause men to be gathered together to strengthen Helaman’s armies.

l: people of Nephi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The people of Nephi are told by Moroni about Helaman’s success so that they may rejoice.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The Lamanites attack the people of Nephihah and begin killing them with an exceedingly great slaughter. Their armies are strengthened by people who had fled from Manti and the surrounding land, and they take the city of Nephihah.

l: people of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The people of Nephihah are attacked by the Lamanites. The remainder of them are forced to flee and join the army of Moroni.

l: armies of Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Moroni seeks to have men gathered to strengthen Helaman’s armies so they can maintain the lands Helaman regained.

l: armies of the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The remainder of the people of Nephihah flee and join the army of Moroni.

l: government, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Moroni becomes angry with the government because of its indifference concerning the freedom of their country.

l: Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Nephihah is attacked and lost to the Lamanites after its people suffer a great slaughter and the remainder flee.

l: epistle, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Moroni sends an epistle to Pahoran requesting that men be gathered to strengthen Helaman’s armies.

l: attack on the people of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The Lamanites attack the people of Nephihah while Moroni is preparing to battle the Lamanites.

l: slaughter of the people of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The Lamanites begin to slay the people of Nephihah with an exceedingly great slaughter.

l: loss of the city of Nephihah, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The city of Nephihah is lost to the Lamanites, causing Moroni and his chief captains to become exceedingly sorrowful, doubtful, and amazed.

l: freedom, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: Moroni is angry with the government because of its indifference concerning the freedom of their country.

l: wickedness of the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 59
s: The wickedness of the people causes Moroni and his chief captains to doubt whether they will fall into the hands of their brethren.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Moroni writes a letter to Pahoran, the chief judge and governor in Zarahemla, condemning the government for neglecting the armies and failing to send provisions and men. He describes the suffering, hunger, slaughter, and deaths among the people while the Lamanites take lands, murder people, and carry women and children captive. Moroni warns that the judgments of God and the sword of justice will come upon the government unless it repents, supports the armies, and defends the country and its freedom. He declares that he seeks neither power nor worldly honor, but the glory of God and the freedom and welfare of his country.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Moroni writes to Pahoran and condemns the government for neglecting the armies, withholding provisions, and allowing thousands to fall. He demands repentance and support for the armies, and threatens to come to Zarahemla with the sword if the government does not act.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Pahoran is the chief judge and governor over the land and is the recipient of Moroni's letter.

l: Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Helaman and his men suffer hunger, thirst, fatigue, and other afflictions. Moroni asks that food and men be sent to Helaman so he can support the parts of the country he has regained.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: God is described as knowing the cries and sufferings of those who have fallen. Moroni fears God, follows his commandments, and says that God will not allow the righteous people to perish with hunger.

l: Lord, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The Lord allows the righteous to be slain so that justice and judgment may come upon the wicked, and the righteous enter into his rest. The Lord has provided means for the people and will not spare governors who refuse to repent.

l: the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The people chose governors to manage the affairs of the war. Thousands of the people suffer and fall by the sword because of neglect, internal conflict, and the attacks of the Lamanites.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The Lamanites come upon the people, take possession of their lands, murder their people, and carry women and children away captive. Their hatred is connected to the tradition of their fathers and has been increased by dissenters.

l: king-men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The king-men desire power and authority and caused bloodshed by taking up their swords against the people. Their actions weakened the people while they were contending with the Lamanites.

l: government, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The government is condemned for slothfulness, neglect, withholding provisions, and failing to send men to strengthen the armies. Moroni warns that the government must repent or face destruction and opposition from him.

l: Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The armies suffer from hunger, thirst, fatigue, lack of provisions, and insufficient strength. Moroni demands that they receive food and men so they can defend the country and recover its possessions.

l: enemies, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The enemies spread death, murder the people, and gain possession of lands when the people are weakened by neglect and internal conflict.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Zarahemla is the city where Pahoran serves as chief judge and governor. Moroni says he will come there and confront the government if it does not provide assistance.

l: land of Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The land is threatened by the Lamanites, who take possession of its lands. Its borders contain people who are wounded, bleeding, and falling by the sword.

l: country, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The country is defended by Moroni and his men, who seek its freedom and welfare. Moroni says the people should unite to defend the country and their little ones.

l: the war, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The war causes great suffering and slaughter, and the people are weakened by a war that also broke out among themselves. Moroni says they cannot successfully contend with the Lamanites until the head of the government is cleansed.

l: the slaughter, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The slaughter among the people is great, with thousands falling by the sword. Moroni attributes much of this loss to the government's failure to provide sufficient strength and support.

l: the letter, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The letter is written by Moroni to Pahoran and the governors. It condemns their neglect and calls for repentance, provisions, men, and a true spirit of freedom.

l: the sword, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The sword causes the deaths of thousands and is used by the Lamanites against the people. Moroni says he will take up the sword against the government if necessary to defend freedom and obtain food.

l: provisions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Provisions have not been sent sufficiently to the armies, contributing to hunger and death. Moroni demands that provisions be sent speedily to him and Helaman.

l: provisions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The armies suffer and nearly perish with hunger because food is withheld. Moroni demands food for their support and says God will provide it even if it must be obtained by the sword.

l: men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Moroni demands that men be sent to strengthen the armies. He also asks that men be sent to Helaman so he can support the recovered parts of the country.

l: commandments of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Moroni is constrained by his covenant to keep the commandments of God. He says he takes up his sword according to those commandments to defend the cause of his country.

l: freedom, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Freedom is the cause Moroni defends and the government is urged to support. Moroni says he seeks the freedom and welfare of his country rather than power or worldly honor.

l: power and authority, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The king-men seek power and authority over the people, causing bloodshed and weakening the defense against the Lamanites. Moroni warns that those who seek to usurp power and authority must become extinct.

l: iniquity, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Wickedness begins at the head of the people and prevents them from withstanding their enemies. The wickedness of those seeking power and authority causes suffering, loss, and destruction.

l: the judgments of God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Moroni fears that the judgments of God will come upon the people because of the government's slothfulness and neglect. He says the righteous may be slain while judgment comes upon the wicked.

l: the sword of justice, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The sword of justice hangs over the government because it fails to defend the country and its little ones. Moroni warns that it will fall upon them and bring utter destruction unless they act.

l: neglect, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Neglect by the government causes the armies to lack strength, provisions, and support. Moroni says this neglect brings the blood and suffering of thousands upon the governors' heads.

l: slothfulness, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: The slothfulness of the government leads to great neglect toward the people and armies. Moroni fears it will bring the judgments of God upon the people.

l: afflictions of the people, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Moroni, his men, Helaman, and Helaman's men suffer hunger, thirst, fatigue, and many afflictions. The people also suffer as the Lamanites murder them and carry women and children captive.

l: temporal death, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 60
s: Death spreads among the people as enemies murder thousands and many fall by the sword. Moroni says the deaths could have been reduced if the government had provided sufficient strength and succor.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Pahoran writes to Moroni explaining that rebels have driven him from the judgment-seat and taken Zarahemla, where they appointed a king and formed an alliance with the Lamanites. Pahoran has fled to Gideon, gathered freemen, and plans to resist the rebels and reclaim Zarahemla. He asks Moroni to come with a few men while Lehi and Teancum continue conducting the war. Pahoran says God will deliver those who stand fast in the liberty and freedom God has given them.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Moroni receives Pahoran’s epistle, in which Pahoran says he does not seek power beyond retaining the judgment-seat and asks Moroni to come speedily with a few men. Moroni is told to strengthen Lehi and Teancum in the Lord.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Pahoran, the chief governor, has been driven out by rebels and fled to Gideon with as many men as possible. He gathers freemen, plans to resist the rebels, and asks Moroni to join him in reclaiming Zarahemla.

l: Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Lehi is left with Teancum in charge of conducting the war in that part of the land. Pahoran sends provisions to Lehi and Teancum so they will not perish until Moroni arrives.

l: Teancum, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Teancum is left with Lehi in charge of conducting the war in that part of the land. Pahoran sends provisions to Teancum and Lehi until Moroni can come.

l: God, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: God has made Pahoran and his people free, and Pahoran says they should trust God to deliver them. Pahoran says God does not command them to subject themselves to their enemies and will deliver those who stand fast in liberty.

l: Lamanites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: The Lamanites are allied with the king appointed by the rebels. They are expected by that alliance to conquer the remainder of the land and place the rebel king over the people.

l: freemen, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Freemen are among those whose rights are threatened by the rebels. They flock daily to Pahoran in defense of their country and freedom and to avenge their wrongs.

l: king-men, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: The rebels rise up against Pahoran and those of his people who are freemen, drive Pahoran out, withhold provisions, and daunt the freemen. They take possession of Zarahemla and appoint a king over themselves.

l: king over the rebels, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: The king over the rebels has been appointed in Zarahemla and writes to the king of the Lamanites. He enters an alliance intended to maintain Zarahemla and make him king over the people after the Lamanites conquer the remainder of the land.

l: land of Gideon, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Gideon is the land to which Pahoran flees after being driven out by the rebels. Pahoran gathers men and receives freemen there.

l: Zarahemla, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Zarahemla is taken by the rebels, who appoint a king over it and ally with the Lamanites. Pahoran and Moroni plan to retake the city to obtain more food.

l: judgment-seat, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: The judgment-seat is the position the rebels seek to take from Pahoran. Pahoran says he seeks to retain it only to preserve the rights and liberty of his people.

l: provisions, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: The rebels withhold provisions, preventing freemen from coming to Moroni. Pahoran sends a few provisions to Lehi and Teancum so they will not perish until Moroni arrives.

l: liberty, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Pahoran says his soul stands fast in the liberty in which God has made him and his people free. He asks Moroni and others to resist evil to retain that liberty.

l: freedom, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: The people are urged to defend their country and freedom and to resist rebellions and dissensions. Pahoran describes freedom as a privilege connected with their church and the cause of their Redeemer and God.

l: rebellion, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Rebellion against Pahoran causes great iniquity and drives him from the judgment-seat. Pahoran says rebellions that cannot be resisted with words should be resisted with swords.

l: alliance, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: An alliance is formed between the king appointed by the rebels and the king of the Lamanites. It provides for maintaining Zarahemla and enabling the Lamanites to conquer the remainder of the land.

l: war against the Nephites, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Lehi and Teancum are left with power to conduct the war in their part of the land according to the Spirit of God and freedom. Moroni is asked to gather forces so he and Pahoran can go against the dissenters.

l: iniquity, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: The rebels’ actions, including taking Zarahemla and allying with the Lamanites, are described as causing great iniquity. Pahoran intends to end this iniquity by reclaiming the city.

l: evil, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 61
s: Pahoran asks Moroni and the people to resist evil, using words where possible and swords against rebellions and dissensions when necessary.

l: The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Moroni joins Pahoran to defeat Pachus, restore Pahoran to the judgment-seat, and enforce the law against those who fight against the freedom of their country. Moroni and Pahoran capture the city of Nephihah, while many Lamanite prisoners join the people of Ammon. Teancum dies while attacking Ammoron, and Moroni, Lehi, and their armies drive the Lamanites from the land. Peace is restored, the church of God is reestablished, and the people of Nephi prosper until Helaman dies in the thirty and fifth year of the reign of the judges.

l: Moroni, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Moroni took a small number of men, gathered more under the standard of liberty, and joined Pahoran in defeating Pachus and restoring Pahoran to the judgment-seat. He captured the city of Nephihah without losing a Nephite, pursued the Lamanites with Lehi and Teancum, mourned Teancum's death, defeated the Lamanites, fortified the land, and later gave command of his armies to his son Moronihah.

l: Pahoran, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Pahoran was driven from the judgment-seat by Pachus and his men, then joined Moroni in defeating them and was restored to the judgment-seat. He later marched with Moroni toward the land of Nephihah and helped obtain possession of the city.

l: Lehi, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Lehi was given command over part of Moroni's army with Teancum. He later joined Moroni in pursuing the Lamanites and was exceedingly sorrowful when Teancum died.

l: Teancum, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Teancum was given command over part of Moroni's army and later encamped with Lehi and Moroni against the Lamanites. In anger toward Ammoron, he entered the Lamanite camp and wounded Ammoron with a javelin, but Ammoron's servants pursued and slew him.

l: Helaman, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Helaman received an army of six thousand men and provisions to assist him in preserving his part of the land. He returned to the place of his inheritance, resumed preaching the word of God, helped reestablish the church of God, and died in the thirty and fifth year of the reign of the judges.

l: Pachus, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Pachus was the king of the dissenters who drove the freemen from the land of Zarahemla and took possession of it. He was slain by Moroni and Pahoran's armies.

l: Ammoron, The Book of Alma, the Son of Alma, Chapter 62
s: Ammoron, the king of the Lamanites, was with the Lamanite armies in the land of Moroni. Teancum cast a javelin at him and pierced him near the heart, and Ammoron's servants then slew Teancum before Ammoron died.
